source.title: Flash STU: Fast Spectral Transform Units
source.authors: Y. I. Liu; Windsor Nguyen; Yagiz Devre; Evan Dogariu; Anirudha Majumdar; Elad Hazan

record.tranche_reason: The study compares validation loss across different architectures at approximately matched parameter counts, bearing on whether architecture details have little effect. It does not fit or test the original scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The paper reports language-model validation losses for architecture comparisons, which bear on V4. It also shows training curves at different scales, but does not fit power laws, test extrapolation, or investigate compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. Downstream benchmark scores are reported, but there is no analysis of whether those scores improve predictably with scale or pretraining loss. Robotics width/depth ablations use a different task and loss measure and do not hold parameter count fixed.
record.test_reason: This is an architecture-proposal paper. It uses Hoffmann et al. to pick about 500M parameters as compute-optimal for 10B tokens, then reports its own model's validation loss against baselines. V4 concerns shape (depth, width and similar details) within an architecture family at fixed parameter count. Comparing different architecture classes (spectral SSM hybrid, Mamba-2, Transformer) measures a different question. No power-law fits, extrapolation, allocation sweeps or loss-to-downstream analysis appear.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that Flash STU is a viable, competitive alternative to Transformers and SSMs, and claim it consistently outperforms them at a fixed parameter budget across synthetic, robotics and language tasks.
record.recipe_differences: This is an architecture comparison, not a reproduction of the scaling-law measurements or fitting procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that Transformer training was more sensitive to hyperparameter tuning, such as learning rate, and more prone to loss spikes than Flash STU.

fits_no_version.finding: At about 550M parameters and 10B FineWeb-Edu tokens, validation loss differs across architecture classes: Flash STU 3.40, Mamba-2 Hybrid 3.44, Mamba-2 3.63, Transformer 3.92. At 2B, Flash STU scores 3.09 vs Transformer 3.18. Baselines are not tuned and training is fixed at 16 GPU-hours.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: At matched parameter count and data, the choice of sequence-mixing architecture class (attention vs SSM vs hybrid) shifts pretraining loss noticeably.

fits_no_version.finding: In MuJoCo Ant-v1 next-state prediction, MSE falls as width or depth (and parameter count) grows for STU, STU-T and Transformer (Tables VIII–X). The Transformer plateaus with depth, and no fit is made.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Loss in robotics next-state prediction decreases with model size, at rates that differ by architecture.

record.peer_reviewed: IEEE Conference on Decision and Control
record.problems: The architecture comparisons are limited in number; the reported validation losses have no uncertainty estimates; and the models are approximately, not exactly, parameter-matched.
record.rows_left_out: No additional qualifying rows left out. The downstream benchmark results in Table III do not test predictability from scale or pretraining loss.

untested.parts: No power-law fits of loss in parameters, tokens or compute.
No extrapolation from small to large runs.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep; Chinchilla ratio only used to choose model size.
No depth/width/shape sweep at fixed parameter count for language models. Robotics width/depth ablations change parameter count.
Robotics and synthetic tasks are reported, but no power-law form is fitted.
Downstream scores (Table III) are given for one size only; no scale or loss trend.
No comparison of fitting choices or exponents.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V4 labels were dropped. Kaplan's V4 is about shape within the Transformer family, while these rows compare different architecture classes in the authors' own-method evaluation, with no uncertainty and limited baseline tuning. The paper cites both originals; Hoffmann is used only to set model size.

versions.untested_parts: No power-law fits for held-out language-model loss against parameters, tokens, or compute.
No predictions from smaller runs are compared with substantially larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or fitted parameter/token growth trends.
The comparisons cover a few architectures at approximate parameter matches, not a broad sweep of depth, width, and other design choices at fixed parameter count.
The paper includes robotics and synthetic tasks but does not test whether a power-law form transfers across modalities or training regimes.
Downstream scores are reported, but their predictability from scale or pretraining loss is not tested.
No comparison of scaling-law fits, exponents, or fitting choices.
